metadata.file_name: 14. Choi & Sung. (2024). Do Key Predictors of Academic Resilience Differ Across Cultures? Evidence From Korea and the US.pdf
metadata.title: Do Key Predictors of Academic Resilience Differ Across Cultures? Evidence From Korea and the US

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-old students in South Korea and the United States, then restricts the analytic sample to students in the bottom 25% of ESCS within each country. The dependent variable is a binary indicator of reading resilience (at or above Level 3 in reading literacy, coded 1, among students in the bottom ESCS quartile, coded 0 otherwise). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling weights or replicate weights in the random forest estimation; instead it describes model fitting in R using the randomForest package and performance evaluation (sensitivity, specificity, accuracy) across 10 plausible-value-based models. Missing values are imputed using na.roughfix (mode for categorical, median for continuous), but the paper does not specify any complex-survey-weight adjustments for the ML models.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student data for reading literacy. Restricted to students in the bottom 25% of ESCS within each country (South Korea and the US). Defined academic resilience as achieving at or above Level 3 in reading literacy while belonging to the bottom 25% of ESCS; created a binary DV (resilient=1, non-resilient=0).

confounders_identified.variable_name: Disciplinary climate in test language lessons
Teacher support in test language lessons

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (15-year-olds), South Korea & United States (bottom 25% ESCS subset)
main_findings.target_variable: Academic resilience (binary: Level 3+ reading among bottom-ESCS students)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (R randomForest, 5,000 trees). Performance across 10 plausible-value-based models: Korea sensitivity 0.68–0.78, specificity 0.72–0.78, accuracy 0.71–0.76; US sensitivity 0.83–0.92, specificity 0.50–0.65, accuracy 0.73–0.79. Variable importance via %IncMSE permutation; final rankings averaged across plausible values.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading the study leveraged meta-cognition (METASUM, UNDREM, METASPAM), reading self-concept (SCREADCOMP), and joy of reading (JOYREAD) to predict academic resilience (Level 3+ reading among bottom-ESCS students), finding that individual-level factors were consistently ranked highest in both South Korea and the United States. This indicates that strengthening reading-related metacognitive skills and positive reading engagement for socioeconomically disadvantaged students may be a cross-cultural priority, while country-specific supports (e.g., self-efficacy/expectations in Korea; fixed mindset/meaning in life in the US) should be tailored rather than assumed universal, though causality cannot be inferred from cross-sectional ML feature importance.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2018 reading literacy to model academic resilience as a binary outcome: students in the bottom 25% of ESCS who achieve at or above Level 3 in reading. Random forest models were fit separately for South Korea and the US on the restricted samples (KOR n=1,654; USA n=1,175), using 10 plausible values for reading and averaging variable-importance rankings across plausible-value-based models. Model performance was moderate: in Korea, sensitivity ranged 0.68–0.78, specificity 0.72–0.78, and accuracy 0.71–0.76; in the US, sensitivity ranged 0.83–0.92, specificity 0.50–0.65, and accuracy 0.73–0.79. The most influential predictors were largely individual factors (especially meta-cognition and joy of reading), while some predictors differed by country (e.g., self-efficacy and educational expectations in Korea; fixed mindset and meaning in life in the US). The paper is cross-sectional and uses ML feature importance (permutation %IncMSE), so results should be interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects, and the manuscript does not report complex-survey weight application for the ML models.
